title: Freight transport
description: Physical process of transporting commodities and merchandise goods and cargo
wiki_lead: Freight transport, also referred to as freight forwarding, is the physical process of transporting commercial products and merchandise goods and cargo. This is by different transportation modes, including air, water, railways, pipelines, and road transports. Pipelines transport items that are liquid and gaseous in nature, while air, water, and roads are used to transport goods and passengers.
wiki_excerpt:
Freight transport, also referred to as freight forwarding, is the physical process of transporting commercial products and merchandise goods and cargo. This is by different transportation modes, including air, water, railways, pipelines, and road transports. Pipelines transport items that are liquid and gaseous in nature, while air, water, and roads are used to transport goods and passengers.


History


Prehistoric era
Initial human civilization relied heavily on domesticated animals, such as horses, camels, and donkeys, to transport their goods. The invention of the wheel in Mesopotamia in 5000 B.C.E improved this efficiency by allowing for carts and carriages to be created, which animals could pull.
Water transport also developed, with a terra-cotta model of a boat from the Ubaid period, circa 4000 BCE, providing some of the earliest evidence for sailboats.


Classical era


Romans
The Romans built a vast network of roads, which facilitated trade across the numerous cities in its empire.


Silk Road

Transport along the silk road, a land-based route, was generally done through caravans, equipped with camels that would carry goods. It was uncommon for traders to traverse the entirety of the silk road — they would pass on their goods to other traders along different legs of the journey.
While silk flowed westward from China, other goods such as wools, gold, and silver were transported east from the West.


Medieval period


Modern period


Industrial Revolution
Freight transport in the UK was shaped significantly by the Industrial Revolution.  A sophisticated canal system in the English Midlands allowed freight to be transported easily over long distances. Additionally, railway systems were popularized; they initially consisted of horse-drawn carts, but switched to steam-powered trains later on.


Aviation
After the invention of the plane by the Wright Brothers, the first air freight shipment was delivered in 1910. While the industry and demand for air freight delivery remained low throughout much of the 20th century, the creation of FedEx in 1973 revolutionised the industry by introducing specialised cargo flights, rather than aggregating passenger and cargo flights in one trip.


Autonomous transportation
Autonomous vehicles have been tested by companies for freight transportation, with potential benefits including reduced labour costs and changes in transport operations. Autonomous delivery robots have also been studied as a way to automate the last mile of the delivery process. A 2024 literature review examined research on these robots, including their potential applications and challenges in last-mile logistics.


Modes of shipment

In 2015, 108 trillion tonne-kilometers were transported worldwide (anticipated to grow by 3.4% per year until 2050 (128 trillion in 2020)): 70% by sea, 18% by road, 9% by rail, 2% by inland waterways and less than 0.25% by air.


Grounds

Land or "ground" shipping can be made by train or by truck (British English: lorry). Ground transport is typically more affordable than air, but more expensive than sea, especially in developing countries, where inland infrastructure may not be efficient. In air and sea shipments, ground transport is required to take the cargo from its place of origin to the airport or seaport and then to its destination because it is not always possible to establish a production facility near ports due to the limited coastlines of countries.


Ship

Much freight transport is done by cargo ships. An individual nation's fleet and the people that crew it are referred to as its merchant navy or merchant marine. According to a 2018 report from the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD), merchant shipping (or seaborne trade) carries 80–90% of international trade and 60–70% by value. On rivers and canals, barges are often used to carry bulk cargo.


Air

Cargo is commonly transported by air in specialized cargo aircraft and in the luggage compartments of passe
grok_lead: Freight transport (Spanish: transporte de carga) is the physical process of moving commodities, merchandise, or goods from one location to another for a fee, typically in bulk quantities, using various modes such as road (trucks), rail, water (ships and barges), air, and pipelines. It encompasses the collection, transportation, transshipment, storage, and delivery of these goods as a key element of logistics and supply chains. This sector underpins global trade and economic activity, with billions of tons of cargo transported annually by trucks, trains, ships, and aircraft to connect producers, consumers, and markets worldwide. In 2020, global freight activity reached approximately 140 billion tonne-kilometers, a figure projected to triple by 2050 amid rising demand from economic growth in regions like Asia, Africa, and Latin America. In the United States, as of 2023, freight transportation handled approximately 20.3 billion tons, supporting about 6.7 million jobs in transportation and warehousing, and contributing roughly 8.7% to the nation's gross domestic product through business logistics costs. The choice of transport mode depends on factors like distance, cargo type, cost, speed, and capacity, leading to competition and complementarity among options. Trucks dominate for flexibility and short-haul distribution, carrying 64% of U.S. freight tonnage but emitting the majority of sector greenhouse gases. Rail excels in high-capacity, long-distance bulk movement, handling 9% of U.S. tonnage at lower environmental cost per ton. Maritime transport, including ocean shipping and inland waterways, moves over 70% of global trade volume for cost-effective international bulk cargo, though it involves high terminal infrastructure needs. Air freight is reserved for time-sensitive, high-value items due to its speed, despite comprising less than 1% of tonnage. Pipelines provide efficient, low-maintenance transport for liquids and gases, accounting for 18% of U.S. tonnage. Effective freight management optimizes routes, modes, and carriers to reduce costs, ensure timely delivery, manage inventory, and minimize environmental risks, while governments invest in infrastructure to handle growing demand projected to increase 40% in U.S. tonnage by 2045. However, the sector contributes about 8% of global greenhouse gas emissions âprimarily from road transport âand faces challenges like supply chain disruptions, requiring shifts toward sustainable practices such as intermodal integration and low-carbon technologies.
